newsitem.title: UK: P&U struggles to rebuild credibility.
newsitem.headline: P&U struggles to rebuild credibility.

text.p: International drugs group Pharmacia & Upjohn Inc was struggling to rebuild its fortunes and credibility on Tuesday after confirming a sharp drop in first-quarter sales and profits.

In contrast with strong performances by all its major competitors, the Swedish-U.S. company said sales fell by 6.1 percent in the first three months of the year to $1.635 billion, while net earnings per share before exceptional items slid 16 percent to $0.37.
The bad news had already been flagged by the group last Wednesday, precipitating a 15 percent drop in the group's share price in Stockholm and a similar plunge in New York.

A bid to dispel the gloom by outlining a recovery strategy however failed to impress beleaguered investors, and group shares continued to trade close their lowest-ever levels in both Stockholm and New York.
Its shares ended unchanged at 219 Swedish crowns in Stockholm on Tuesday, but were down 5/8 at $28 in afternoon trade in New York.
"It is just one disappointment after another," said Salomon Brothers analyst Robert Uhl.
Every section of the business saw sales either drop or stand still.

Pharmacia & Upjohn blamed currency factors for the bulk of the fall in sales, and announced plans to improve currency hedging to protect itself from exchange rate movements. But analysts were not convinced by the explanation, and were particularly worried by the deterioration in sales of older products which have lost patent protection.
New drugs, including glaucoma treatment Xalatan and colo-rectal cancer product Camptosar, saw rapid growth, but not fast enough to override falls elsewhere.

The results were the latest blow to a company which has been hit by three profit warnings in six months, speculation about a clash of cultures, and the abrupt departure of its chief executive officer, John Zabriskie, in January.

Pharmacia & Upjohn was formed in November 1995 with high hopes of being one of the world's top ten in terms of sales, but figures from information group IMS showed it trailing in 17th place last year.

Both partners in the group were known to have approached other companies before settling on each other, and board chairman Richard Brown was forced to defend the rationale behind the merger on Tuesday.

"It made sense when we agreed to do it and it makes as much sense today," he said. Expressing dissatisfaction and disappointment with the results he added that the company's top priorities were restoring confidence and enhancing long-term shareholder value.
However, managers held out little prospect of a marked turnaround in the rest of 1997.

The group has failed to deliver on another key promise at the time of merger, back-pedalling on predictions of annual cost-savings of $500 million by 1998, which acting chief executive Jan Ekberg admitted had been "too aggressive".
Ekberg set out plans to "significantly improve short-and long-term results", and said the search for a new chief executive was at an advanced stage.
Among initiatives announced by Pharmacia & Upjohn were plans to focus resources on the launch and marketing of new products and concentrate on core prescription pharmaceuticals operations.
The plans, which were short on detail, also included refocusing the drug portfolio, cutting costs, based on benchmarking against competitors, and better management of assets.

"I see nothing in the results which could explain just how bad they are, and nothing in the plans for the future that will change this situation," said Daiwa analyst Nigel Keegan, who now rates the group's shares "an out-and-out sell".
